stepsRecall the moments of inertia of a solid sphere (2/5 MR2) and a thin hollow sphere (2/3 MR2) about a diameter → Use I = MK2 to express each radius of gyration and take their ratio (a square root of the ratio of the moments of inertia)

ConceptRadius of gyration is k=I/M, so comparing a solid sphere (I=25MR2) with a thin shell (I=23MR2) means comparing square roots, not the coefficients themselves
Why this answerThis question requires two stored moments of inertia turned into radii of gyration and divided in the stem's order, demonstrated by the stem asking for "the ratio of radius of gyration of a solid sphere ... to the radius of gyration of the thin hollow sphere of same mass and radius".
NoteThe key is tagged as printed, and a doubt is recorded rather than acted on: k=I/M, so the ratio of the two radii of gyration is 3:5, while the printed option 4, 3:5, is the ratio of k2 (equivalently of the two moments of inertia). No option carries 3:5, so the key is the only available choice and the labels follow it; a reviewer should log this as a square root dropped in the question rather than in the key.
What catches a student
The trapoption 1Reversedreversedthe right thing stated backwards: direction, order or ratio

The two coefficients 25 and 23 divided in the order they were written down, shell over sphere, give 2/32/5=53, which is the printed ratio turned the other way up.

Who fallsa student who has both moments of inertia memorised and sets up the quotient from the formula sheet rather than from the stem's order

Why it feels rightthe stem names the solid sphere first and the hollow sphere second, and 5:3 is the quotient of the same two numbers, so the arithmetic looks confirmed and only the order is at stake

  1. okSolid sphere I=25MR2, thin shell I=23MR2.
  2. badDividing the shell's 23 by the sphere's 25 gives 5:3.The stem asks for the solid sphere's value divided by the hollow sphere's, so the 25 goes on top: 2/52/3=35.
Also pullsoption 2

Who fallsa student who recalls the solid sphere's coefficient first and reads the question as asking for that coefficient

Why it feels right2:5 is the numbers in 25MR2 printed as a ratio, and the stem's first-named body is the solid sphere

  1. okThe solid sphere about its own axis has I=25MR2.
  2. badSo the ratio asked for is 2:5.A ratio needs both bodies in it; the shell's 23 has to divide the sphere's 25 before anything is read off.
No route to itoption 3

Checked every quotient the two coefficients allow: 2/52/3=3:5, its inverse 5:3, and the bare coefficient 2:5 - all three are printed. 5:2 is none of them; it requires the bare coefficient to be formed AND then inverted, two separate moves on a number that was never a ratio of the two bodies. It completes the spread as the mirror of option 2.

The work functions of Caesium (Cs), Potassium (K) and Sodium (Na) are 2.14 eV, 2.30 eV and 2.75 eV respectively. If incident electromagnetic radiation has an incident energy of 2.20 eV, which of these photosensitive surfaces may emit photoelectrons?
  1. Both Na and K
  2. K only
  3. Na only
  4. Cs only
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Photoelectrons are emitted only if Ephoton ≥ φ.
  2. Cs: φ = 2.14 eV < 2.20 eV, so Cs emits.
  3. K: φ = 2.30 eV > 2.20 eV, so K does not emit.
  4. Na: φ = 2.75 eV > 2.20 eV, so Na does not emit.
  5. Only Cs emits, which is option 4.

stepsRecall the photoelectric condition that emission requires photon energy at least equal to the work function, and compare 2.20 eV against each of the three given work functions
why it is trickyThe work is a single recalled condition (E >= work function) applied as a direct numerical comparison of 2.20 eV with three stated values; no calculation is needed.

Categories
TypeMCQmcqa question and four answers, nothing lettered or listed
AsksRule appliedapply_rulea rule you already know, used on a case you have not seen
ConceptPhotoemission needs the photon energy to reach or exceed the work function, so only the surface whose work function lies below the incident energy emits
Why this answerThis question requires the threshold condition applied to three supplied work functions with no quantity produced, demonstrated by the stem "If incident electromagnetic radiation has an incident energy of 2.20 eV, which of these photosensitive surfaces may emit photoelectrons?" against the printed 2.14, 2.30 and 2.75 eV.
What catches a student
The trapoption 1Reversedreversedthe right thing stated backwards: direction, order or ratio

Reading the threshold as "the work function must exceed the photon energy" admits exactly the two surfaces whose printed values sit above 2.20 eV, K at 2.30 and Na at 2.75, which is option 1 complete.

Who fallsa student who has the photoelectric condition as an inequality between two energies but has not fixed which side must be the larger

Why it feels rightthe option gathers the two metals whose numbers are bigger than the given energy, so it looks like the result of a comparison carried out carefully on all three values

  1. okEmission is decided by comparing the incident 2.20 eV with each work function.
  2. badA surface emits when its work function is greater than the incident energy, so Na (2.75) and K (2.30) emit.The photon has to pay the work function: emission needs E ≥ φ, which only Cs at 2.14 eV satisfies.
No route to itoption 2

K's printed work function is 2.30 eV, above the incident 2.20 eV, so K emits on no correct reading of the inequality. On the reversed reading that produces option 1, K qualifies but so does Na, so reaching "K only" needs the inequality inverted and then Na discarded as well - two moves, where option 1 is the whole result of the first. Checked both directions of the comparison against all three printed values.

No route to itoption 3

Na's 2.75 eV is the furthest of the three above the incident 2.20 eV, so it fails the condition by the widest margin; and on the reversed reading it qualifies only together with K. Like option 2 it needs the inversion plus a discard, so no single reading of the stem's numbers lands here. The three single-metal options exist as the spread of one name each.

The amount of energy required to form a soap bubble of radius 2 cm from a soap solution is nearly (surface tension of soap solution = 0.03 N m-1)
  1. 5.06 × 10-4 J
  2. 3.01 × 10-4 J
  3. 50.1 × 10-4 J
  4. 30.16 × 10-4 J
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. A soap bubble has two free surfaces, so the area created is A = 2 × 4π r2 = 8π r2.
  2. r = 2 cm = 0.02 m, so r2 = 4 × 10-4 m2.
  3. A = 8π × 4 × 10-4 = 32π × 10-4 m2 ≈ 1.005 × 10-2 m2.
  4. W = T A = 0.03 × 1.005 × 10-2 ≈ 3.016 × 10-4 J.
  5. 3.01 × 10-4 J is option 2.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict

why it is trickyThe work is a recall of W = T x (area created) plus the application that a bubble has two surfaces, followed by a cm-to-m conversion and arithmetic.

  1. Boyle's law at constant n and T: PV = nRT, so P = nRT·1V.
  2. A plot of P against 1V is a straight line through the origin with slope nRT.

  6. Option 4 is P vs V hyperbolas, but the outermost curve is labelled T1 although T3 > T2 > T1; the outermost isotherm should be T3, so the labelling is wrong.

Consider the following compounds/species: [figure: structures i.–vii.] The number of compounds/species which obey Huckel’s rule is ______.
  1. 6
  2. 2
  3. 5
  4. 4
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. i. Naphthalene: planar, cyclic, conjugated with 10 π electrons = 4(2)+2, so it obeys Huckel's rule.
  2. ii. Cyclopentadienyl anion: 4 π electrons from two C=C plus the lone pair gives 6 π electrons = 4(1)+2, so it obeys.
  3. iii. Cyclobutadiene: 4 π electrons = 4n with n=1, antiaromatic, does not obey.
  4. iv. Cyclopropenyl anion: 2 π from C=C plus the lone pair gives 4 π electrons = 4n, does not obey.
  5. v. Cyclopropenyl cation: 2 π electrons = 4(0)+2, so it obeys.
  6. vi. Cyclooctatetraene: 8 π electrons = 4n and tub-shaped (non-planar), does not obey.
  7. vii. Anthracene: 14 π electrons = 4(3)+2, so it obeys.
  8. Species obeying: i, ii, v, vii, so the count is 4, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict

difficultyhard · 5 steps
stepsFor each of the seven species, check that it is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated (decide whether the charged carbon or lone pair joins the π system, and whether the 8-membered ring stays planar) → Count the π electrons in each, including the lone pair on the anions and the empty p orbital on the cation → Treat the fused polycycles (naphthalene, anthracene) by counting the whole periphery π electrons (10 and 14) → Test each count against 4n+2, telling apart the 4-π species (cyclobutadiene, cyclopropenyl anion, cyclooctatetraene with 8) from the 2/6/10/14-π ones → Tally the species that pass and match the total to an option

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Oxidation states: Cr in Cr2O72- is +6, in Cr3+ is +3; S in SO32- is +4, in SO42- is +6.
  2. Electrons gained per Cr2O72-: 2 × 3 = 6; electrons lost per SO32-: 2.
  3. Equate electrons: 6a = 2b ⇒ b = 3a; take a = 1, b = 3.
  4. Charge balance: left -2 - 6 + c, right 2(+3) + 3(-2) = 0, so c - 8 = 0 ⇒ c = 8.
  5. Check oxygen: left 7 + 9 = 16, right 12 + c2 = 12 + 4 = 16. Balanced.
  6. a, b, c = 1, 3, 8, which is option 4.

  1. Synergids are cells of the egg apparatus, formed from the haploid megaspore, so they are haploid (n).

difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsRecall the NCERT chordate vs non-chordate comparison table (nerve cord dorsal/hollow/single vs ventral/solid/double; heart ventral vs dorsal; gill slits present; closed circulation) → Check each of the five statements A-E against that table, catching the mixed-up qualifiers in A (dorsal but solid and double) and D (dorsal heart), and recalling that chordates are coelomate, not pseudocoelomate (E) → Match the set of accepted statements to the option combinations
why it is trickyThe work is recalling one NCERT comparison table and checking five statements against it, two of which splice a chordate word with a non-chordate feature, then matching the surviving set to an option.
the catchStatements A and D each pair a chordate-sounding word ('mid-dorsal', 'dorsal') with a non-chordate feature, so a candidate reading quickly accepts them; option 4 is built from exactly that misreading.

TypeStatementsstatementslettered statements, the answer is which combination is right
AsksStated factfact_linea fact NCERT states: what, who or where
ConceptChordates have a dorsal, hollow, single nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits, a ventral heart, a closed circulation and a true coelom; the solid double nerve cord and the dorsal heart belong to the non-chordates
Why this answerThis question requires the stated chordate characters, demonstrated by statement A's "solid and double nerve cord" and statement D's "Presence of dorsal heart" being the non-chordate entries of the same comparison.
Notereversed was considered, since a dorsal heart is the inversion of a ventral one, and ruled out because one label has to cover the whole option: statement E's pseudocoelom is not an inversion of anything but the body-cavity term of the phyla printed just before Chordata, so what the option is built on throughout is importing from what sits beside the right fact. Swap test agrees — none of the wrong items resembles the right one as a word.

The trapoption 3Neighbouring factnearby_facta true fact about a neighbouring thing is offered instead

The gill slits in C are the chordate character the chapter states most plainly, and the other two items are imported from what is printed beside: the dorsal heart from the non-chordate column of the comparison, and the pseudocoelom from the body cavity of the phyla taught just before Chordata.
